name: Habsburg Monarchy
line: Do your duty early, take your coffee slowly and make music at home.

quote.text: The Café Central is a place for people who want to be alone, but who need company to do it.
quote.source: Theory of the Café Central, 1926. Translated from the German

quotes.text: Let others wage war. You, happy Austria, marry.
quotes.source: Bella gerant alii, tu felix Austria nube. Traditional, 15th or 16th century, on the dynasty’s rise by marriage
Viribus unitis, the personal motto he chose on his accession in December 1848

quotes.text: Truly, if the Austrian empire had not existed for ages, it would be necessary, in the interest of Europe, in the interest of mankind itself, to create it with all speed.
quotes.source: The Czech historian’s letter declining a seat in the Frankfurt Parliament, 11 April 1848

quotes.text: When I attempt to find a simple formula for the period in which I grew up, prior to the First World War, I hope that I convey its fullness by calling it the Golden Age of Security.
quotes.source: The World of Yesterday, 1942, opening of chapter 1, in the English translation of 1943

quotes.text: You have worries, of one kind or another: to the coffeehouse.
quotes.source: From his prose poem Kaffeehaus, 1918. Translated from the German

quotes.text: I am spared nothing in this world.
quotes.source: On being told of the murder of the Empress Elisabeth, 10 September 1898, as reported by his adjutant

words.usage: From Caesar. The head of the house was Holy Roman Emperor for most of four centuries and Emperor of Austria from 1804.
Kaiserlich und königlich: the label on everything shared by Austria and Hungary after 1867, from the army to the tobacco shops.
The sprawling winter palace in the middle of Vienna, added to by every generation for six hundred years.
Franz Joseph’s ruling idea. He called himself the first servant of his state and worked at his desk daily for sixty-eight years.
The official, in uniform, who held the empire together from Trieste to Galicia. Honest, slow and proud of his files.
A senior civil service title, still awarded in Austria and still used when addressing its holder and his wife.
The settlement of 1867 that made Hungary an equal partner, creating the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary.
One of the seventeen provinces of the Austrian half, each with its own diet, capital and coat of arms.
Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Ukrainians, Romanians, Croats, Serbs, Slovaks, Slovenes and Italians under one crown.
The second living room of the Viennese. One orders a coffee and may stay all day with the newspapers.
The standard Viennese order: half coffee, half hot milk, with foam.

words.meaning: Black coffee with whipped cream, in a glass
words.usage: Named after the one-horse cab. The cream kept it warm for drivers waiting in the cold.
The way to address a coffeehouse waiter, who wears a dinner jacket and knows every regular’s order.
A guest with his own table and his own hour. Writers gave the cafe as their postal address.
Coffee and cake, or bread and cold meats, at about four.

words.meaning: A flour dish; a pastry or pudding
words.usage: The Austrian word for the whole kingdom of strudels, dumplings, pancakes and cakes, which could be a meal in themselves.
A room, an evening or a person that makes you comfortable and in no hurry to leave.
Charm, irony and a little gentle deception, all at once. A way of speaking that never quite says what it means.
A greeting to a lady, usually only spoken. Still heard from older gentlemen and waiters.
Literally your servant. Used across the old empire, and still in Austria, Hungary, Slovakia, Croatia and Transylvania.
The daily stroll, properly dressed, in the park or along the boulevard.
The hour when the whole town walks up and down the main street to see and be seen. Every city of the monarchy had one.
An imperial hunting ground that Joseph II opened to the public in 1766. Meadows, a chestnut avenue and a fairground.
The grand circular avenue built from 1857 where Vienna’s walls had stood, lined with the opera, the parliament, the university and the museums.
A turning dance in three-four time that scandalised and then conquered Europe from Vienna.
Vienna still holds some four hundred each winter, given by every profession from the doctors to the chimney sweeps.
Family and friends playing and singing together in the drawing room. The source of most of the chamber music of the age.
Plain, graceful furniture and a quiet private life under a watchful police state.

words.meaning: This year’s wine; a wine tavern
words.usage: Growers in the villages round Vienna may sell their own new wine at home. A green branch over the door shows they are open.
A prime minister’s cheerful description of how the monarchy was governed: keep everyone in a state of even, moderate discontent.

practices.name: At the desk at five
practices.instructions: Rise early, wash in cold water and be at your desk before the rest of the house is up. Take the pile of things awaiting your decision, letters, forms, requests, bills, and go through them in order, one at a time. Read each properly, decide, and write the answer. Do not skip the dull ones. The rule of this Onda is to begin early and do your duty first. If five is too early, choose your own fixed hour.
practices.why: Emperor Franz Joseph rose at half past three or four and worked at his desk for hours. His example set the tone of the Habsburg bureaucracy: the first servant of the state.
variations: Work for thirty minutes at a fixed hour.
Finish with a cup of coffee.

practices.name: A phrase in your neighbour’s tongue
practices.instructions: Choose a language spoken by people you live or work among, or by a neighbouring country, that is not your own. Learn one useful phrase in it today: a greeting, thanks, how are you, a toast. Say it aloud until it is easy, then use it on someone. The rule of this Onda is to learn the other person’s language.
practices.why: The Habsburg lands had a dozen languages, and educated people knew several. Trying a neighbour’s language is a mark of courtesy.
variations: Learn a phrase in Czech, Hungarian or Italian.
Ask a neighbour to teach you.

practices.name: Address them properly
practices.instructions: Address each person you meet today with their proper form: Herr Doktor, Frau Professor, Mr Smith, Ms Jones. Habsburg Vienna loved titles, even ludicrous ones like Frau Hofrat. Use the name or title the person prefers, and add a polite phrase, such as küss die Hand or servus. Notice what it does to the room. Be courteous to everyone.
practices.why: Titles and forms of address were a social art in the Habsburg lands. Courtesy costs nothing and brightens most days.
variations: Use a title for someone who does not expect it.
Learn how a colleague likes to be called.
Say please and thank you in two languages.

practices.name: Kipferl and coffee
practices.instructions: Eat a simple Viennese breakfast: a fresh roll or kipferl, butter, jam and a cup of coffee with a glass of water. Sit down for it. Read the paper while you eat, or just look out of the window. The crescent-shaped kipferl is the ancestor of the croissant. Take time. The rule of this Onda is to take time over coffee.
practices.why: The Viennese breakfast of roll and coffee is a daily pleasure in the former Habsburg lands. It is quick, plain and civilised.
variations: Pour the coffee into a nice cup.

practices.name: A cold wash
practices.instructions: Wash your face and arms with cold water to start the day, as Franz Joseph did every morning. Splash briskly, dry well and feel awake. If cold is not right for you, use cool water. Stand tall afterwards and breathe. It is a small, bracing discipline. Do not do this if you have a heart or blood-pressure condition.
practices.why: A cold wash was a bracing habit of the Emperor, who was famed for his iron discipline. A cool splash is an easy way to start with energy.
variations: Finish a shower with cold water.

practices.name: Count to three in waltz
practices.instructions: Learn the box step of the waltz: forward on the left, side with the right, close; back on the right, side with the left, close. Count one-two-three, one-two-three. Practise in the hall for five minutes with a record of Strauss. Smile at the mirror. The Vienna waltz was the dance of the Habsburg ballrooms.
practices.why: The Viennese waltz took over the Habsburg capital in the 1800s. A box step is enough to begin.

practices.name: An hour in the coffeehouse
practices.instructions: Go to a cafe where you will be left alone. Order one coffee. It should come with a glass of water. Take a newspaper or two, on paper, and read them through, including a page you would normally skip. Then write: a letter, a page of a diary, a poem. Stay for the whole hour, order nothing more unless you want it, and leave a good tip. The coffeehouse table is yours for the hour.
practices.why: The Viennese coffeehouse is a living room for the public. A coffee, a glass of water and a newspaper buy you a table for as long as you like.
variations: Play chess or cards at the table.

practices.name: The promenade
practices.instructions: Late in the afternoon dress properly, as if you might meet someone, and go for a walk with no errand. Choose a park, a river bank or a handsome street. Walk at an easy pace. Greet everyone you know and stop for a word. Look at the buildings and the faces. Walking every day is a rule of this Onda.
practices.why: The promenade, the Korso, was a daily ritual of Habsburg towns, where people walked to see and be seen. A stroll is good for the spirit.
variations: Walk the Ringstrasse of your town.

practices.name: The Jause
practices.instructions: Take a Jause, a mid-afternoon snack, with a cup of coffee or tea and a small cake: a slice of Sachertorte, apple strudel, a poppy-seed roll. Sit down for it. This is the Viennese way to cut the long gap between lunch and dinner. Share a piece with a colleague, and talk about nothing in particular.
practices.why: The Jause is a beloved Austrian ritual, a break in the afternoon with something sweet. It lifts the mood and spreads good cheer.

practices.name: A hand of schnapsen
practices.instructions: Play schnapsen, a two-player card game from Austria, with 20 cards, or any quick trick-taking game. Learn the rules online and play three rounds with a friend. The aim is to score 66 points. Chat as you play, and bow to a good move. Card games were the evening pastime of the Habsburg lands.
practices.why: Schnapsen is one of the most popular two-player card games in Central Europe. It is quick to learn and endlessly rewarding.
variations: Play tarock if you have a group.

practices.name: Schmäh
practices.instructions: Practise Schmäh, the Viennese art of charming, ironical banter. Greet someone with a humorous understatement, a gentle tease or a wry observation. Keep it friendly and never cruel. For example, when someone says it is hot, reply: yes, quite mild for August. See if you can make three people smile.
practices.why: Schmäh is the particular Viennese humour of irony and charm. It lightens everyday dealings and is an art in itself.

practices.name: Twenty minutes with a painting
practices.instructions: Look at one painting properly for twenty minutes: in a gallery, or in a book or online. Try Klimt’s The Kiss, a Bruegel from the Kunsthistorisches Museum, or any work you like. Sit in front of it. Notice colour, composition and detail. Then write three lines about what it says. Vienna’s museums were built for such looking.
practices.why: The Habsburg collections formed the great museums of Vienna, open to the public from the 1700s. A slow look is a luxury anyone can have.
variations: Look at The Hunters in the Snow.

practices.name: Music at home
practices.instructions: Make music in your own home this evening, with whoever is there. Sing a song everyone knows, play duets, pick out a tune on any instrument, or put on a waltz and dance in the kitchen. It does not have to be good. If you are alone, play or sing one piece. The rule of this Onda is to make music, not only hear it.
practices.why: Hausmusik, music made at home, was the heart of Habsburg bourgeois life. Schubert wrote many of his songs for evening parties with friends.
variations: Invite a friend to bring an instrument.

practices.name: A waltz in the kitchen
practices.instructions: Put on a Strauss waltz, such as The Blue Danube, clear a space and dance. Waltz with a partner or a broom. Turn slowly, rise and fall with the music, and finish with a bow. The waltz was a scandal when it first arrived, because dancers held each other close. Now it is a pleasure.
practices.why: The waltz was the dance of the Habsburg world. Strauss’s waltzes are the music of the whole age.

practices.name: An evening with Zweig
practices.instructions: Read a few pages of Stefan Zweig’s memoir of the Vienna of his youth, a world of security and culture that vanished in 1914. Read slowly and aloud. Notice his nostalgia, and ask whether the world was really as safe as he remembers. The book was finished shortly before he died in exile in 1942.
practices.why: The World of Yesterday is the best portrait of the late Habsburg world, written by one of its great citizens in exile. It is both elegy and warning.
variations: Compare it with a memory of your own.

practices.name: A quartet for the evening
practices.instructions: Play Haydn’s Emperor Quartet, which contains the tune later used as Austria’s and Germany’s anthem, in its slow movement. Listen to the four strings in a quiet room with a cup of tea. Notice how the tune is passed from one instrument to another. The tune was written in 1797 to honour Emperor Francis.
practices.why: Haydn’s quartet movement on the Emperor’s Hymn is a perfect piece of chamber music. It has been the German national tune since 1922.

practices.name: Write a letter
practices.instructions: Write a proper letter by hand to a friend or relative. Open with a courteous greeting and close with warm regards. Include news, a joke and a question. Habsburg correspondence was elegant and unhurried. Seal it and post it. Letters kept the far-flung lands of the monarchy together.
practices.why: Letter-writing was an art in the Habsburg lands, with elaborate forms of address. A handwritten letter is a lovely gift.

practices.name: Dress for dinner
practices.instructions: Change for dinner, even if you will eat at home. Put on a clean shirt or a favourite dress, brush your hair and light a candle on the table. The Habsburg town dweller dressed up for the evening meal as a mark of respect for the family. Sit down together and eat slowly. A small change makes a big difference.
practices.why: Dressing for dinner marked the end of the working day. It is a small ceremony that brings a sense of occasion.
variations: Set the table with a cloth.
Say a toast at the start.

practices.name: A Viennese Sunday
practices.instructions: Spend a Sunday in the Viennese way: a lunch of Tafelspitz, boiled beef with root vegetables, horseradish and apple, followed by a promenade in a park, a stop for coffee and cake, and an evening of music. Invite a guest if you like. Dress nicely. Go slowly and enjoy the pace. Nothing else is required.
practices.why: The Viennese Sunday, with its special lunch and its walk, was a family ritual in the Habsburg lands. Recreating it is a happy way to spend a day.
variations: Visit a park and the coffeehouse.
End with a game of cards.

practices.name: A home ball
practices.instructions: Hold a ball at home or in a hall. Dress up, put on waltzes, polkas and a march, and invite friends. Open with a dance, give everyone a card for the dances and learn one new step. Serve something light to eat and a sparkling juice. The Vienna ball season runs from New Year to Shrove Tuesday. Keep the mood graceful and merry.
practices.why: The ball was the high social event of the Habsburg year, with the Opera Ball as the grandest. A small version at home is a joy.
variations: End with the Radetzky March and clapping.

immersePlan.name: Read The World of Yesterday
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Zweig’s memoir. Note one detail of daily life that has changed.

immersePlan.name: Read The Radetzky March
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Joseph Roth’s 1932 novel of three generations of a family loyal to the old monarchy. Notice the irony.

immersePlan.name: Read Danubia
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Simon Winder’s witty history of the Habsburgs. Note one odd fact.

immersePlan.name: Watch Amadeus
immersePlan.text: Watch Miloš Forman’s 1984 film of Mozart in Habsburg Vienna. Listen for the music.

immersePlan.name: Watch Sissi
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1955 film of Empress Elisabeth, beloved in Austrian cinema. Notice how it handles the nostalgia.

immersePlan.name: Watch Colonel Redl
immersePlan.text: Watch István Szabó’s 1985 film about a ambitious army officer in the last years of the monarchy. A serious and haunting story.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Emperor Quartet
immersePlan.text: Play Haydn’s quartet with its slow movement based on the hymn. Follow the tune as it passes between instruments.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Trout Quintet
immersePlan.text: Play Schubert’s quintet with its set of variations on the song of the trout. Enjoy the sparkle.

immersePlan.name: Listen to The Blue Danube
immersePlan.text: Play Johann Strauss’s waltz of 1867 and dance a few bars around the room, however clumsily, with a partner or alone.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Kiss
immersePlan.text: Look at Klimt’s gold-covered painting of two lovers on a flowery meadow. Notice the patterns of their robes.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Bruegel room
immersePlan.text: Look at the Kunsthistorisches Museum’s unmatched collection of Bruegel, including The Hunters in the Snow and The Tower of Babel. Pick one.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Postal Savings Bank
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Otto Wagner’s 1906 bank in Vienna, with aluminium bolts and a glass ceiling. A modern building from the monarchy’s last years.

immersePlan.name: Cook tafelspitz
immersePlan.text: Simmer beef with root vegetables in a good broth and serve with horseradish and apple sauce.

immersePlan.name: Make Wiener schnitzel
immersePlan.text: Beat veal or pork thin, coat in flour, egg and breadcrumbs and fry in butter until golden. Serve with lemon.

immersePlan.name: Make Kaiserschmarrn
immersePlan.text: Make a thick pancake, tear it into pieces as it cooks and serve with sugar, raisins and plum compote. It was the emperor’s favourite.

immersePlan.name: Make a melange
immersePlan.text: Make strong coffee with steamed milk and a spoon of foam. Serve it with a glass of water on a small tray.

immersePlan.name: Make an apple spritzer
immersePlan.text: Mix apple juice and sparkling water half and half with a slice of lemon. It stands in for the white wine spritzer of the Heuriger.

immersePlan.name: Drink golden grape juice
immersePlan.text: Pour a small glass of sweet golden grape juice and sip it as you would Tokaji, the dessert wine of Hungary that Habsburg courts adored.

immersePlan.name: Use proper titles
immersePlan.text: Address everyone today by their proper title or form. Notice how it changes the tone.

immersePlan.name: Stay at the table
immersePlan.text: Sit at a coffeehouse table or your own table for an hour with a single coffee. Nobody will hurry you.

immersePlan.name: Dance one dance
immersePlan.text: Put on a waltz and dance one dance, however clumsily. The ball season runs from New Year to Shrove Tuesday.

immersePlan.name: Play tarock
immersePlan.text: Play the big card game of Austria and Hungary with three players and a deck of 54. Learn the rules online.

immersePlan.name: Play schnapsen
immersePlan.text: Play the quick two-player card game of Austria with twenty cards, racing to 66 points. Chat as you play and enjoy each trick.

immersePlan.name: Play carom billiards
immersePlan.text: Play the game with three balls and no pockets on a table. Or play ordinary pool and score points for caroms.

immersePlan.name: Mark the New Year’s Concert
immersePlan.text: The Vienna Philharmonic plays Strauss on 1 January. Listen to the Radetzky March at the end and clap along.

immersePlan.name: Look up Café Sperl
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 1880 coffeehouse in Vienna, with marble tables and billiards. Imagine an hour there.

immersePlan.name: Look up Schönbrunn
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the imperial summer palace in Vienna, with its gardens and gloriette. Pick a room.

immersePlan.name: Practise Gemütlichkeit
immersePlan.text: Gemütlichkeit is cosiness and good cheer. Make one corner of your home warm and welcoming this evening.

immersePlan.name: Practise Schmäh
immersePlan.text: Schmäh is charming banter. Make three people smile with a witty remark today.

immersePlan.name: Take a Jause
immersePlan.text: Jause is the afternoon snack. Take a break with a small treat and a hot drink, and share it.

rules.text: Begin early and do your duty first
rules.why: Clear what others are waiting on you for before you do anything for yourself.
Greet, thank and give each person their title. Form is a kindness.
A few words in someone’s own tongue are the beginning of living together.
An hour with the newspapers is not wasted. Do not hurry and do not hurry others.
Out of doors, properly dressed, with no purpose but the walk.

rules.text: Make music, do not only hear it
rules.why: Sing or play something each evening, however badly.

read.title: The World of Yesterday
read.creator: Stefan Zweig, trans. Anthea Bell
read.why: A memoir of Vienna before 1914 and of everything that came after, written in exile and posted to the publisher the day before he took his life.

read.title: The Radetzky March
read.creator: Joseph Roth
read.why: Three generations of a family raised up by saving the emperor’s life decline along with the empire. The great novel of the monarchy’s end.

read.title: The Habsburg Empire: A New History
read.creator: Pieter M. Judson
read.why: A history that argues the empire worked better, and was more popular with its peoples, than its obituarists allowed.

read.title: Danubia
read.creator: Simon Winder
read.why: A funny, opinionated ramble through the dynasty’s lands and oddities.

read.title: The Man Without Qualities
read.creator: Robert Musil
read.why: A vast unfinished novel of Vienna in 1913, in which a committee tries to find a great idea for the emperor’s jubilee. He named the country Kakania.

read.title: The Hare with Amber Eyes
read.creator: Edmund de Waal
read.why: A family of Jewish bankers on the Ringstrasse, their palace and what became of them, traced through a collection of small Japanese carvings.

watch.title: Colonel Redl
watch.creator: István Szabó
watch.why: A railwayman’s son rises in the imperial army by loyalty and concealment. A Hungarian film about what the monarchy asked of its servants.

watch.title: Amadeus
watch.creator: Miloš Forman
watch.why: Mozart at the court of Joseph II, as told by his rival. Filmed in Prague, with the emperor a decent man who thinks there are too many notes.

watch.title: Sissi
watch.creator: Ernst Marischka
watch.why: The young Empress Elisabeth as a fairy tale, with Romy Schneider. Wholly sentimental, and shown on Austrian television every Christmas.

watch.title: Corsage
watch.creator: Marie Kreutzer
watch.why: The same empress at forty, bored, watched and laced tight. An antidote to the film above.

listen.title: String Quartet in C, Opus 76 No. 3, the Emperor
listen.creator: Joseph Haydn
listen.why: The slow movement is a set of variations on the hymn he wrote for Emperor Franz. The tune outlived the empire.

listen.title: Piano Quintet in A, the Trout
listen.creator: Franz Schubert
listen.why: Written for a mining official who played the cello, to be performed at home among friends.

listen.title: The Blue Danube
listen.creator: Johann Strauss II
listen.why: The waltz that became Vienna’s second anthem, written in the year of the Compromise.

listen.title: Radetzky March
listen.creator: Johann Strauss I
listen.why: Composed for the field marshal who put down the Italian revolt. It closes the New Year’s Concert each year, with the audience clapping.

art.title: The crown of Rudolf II
art.creator: Jan Vermeyen, court goldsmith in Prague
art.why: A circlet, a high arch and a bishop’s mitre in gold, enamel, pearls and a great sapphire. Later the crown of the Austrian Empire. In the Imperial Treasury, Vienna.

art.title: The Bruegel room
art.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
art.why: The Hunters in the Snow, the Tower of Babel and ten more, gathered by Habsburg archdukes. The largest group of his paintings anywhere, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

art.title: The Kiss
art.creator: Gustav Klimt
art.why: A couple wrapped in gold on a flowered cliff edge. Bought by the state for its new modern gallery before it was finished. In the Belvedere.

art.title: The Postal Savings Bank
art.creator: Otto Wagner
art.why: A public building clad in marble slabs fixed with aluminium bolts, with a glass-roofed hall. Modern architecture begins here, in an imperial ministry.

eat.title: Tafelspitz
eat.creator: Simmered beef with root vegetables, apple horseradish and chive sauce
eat.why: Franz Joseph ate boiled beef at almost every midday meal, and the dish was served throughout the empire on his birthday.

eat.title: Wiener Schnitzel
eat.creator: Veal beaten thin, breaded and fried in butter
eat.why: It should cover the plate and puff away from the meat. Served with lemon and potato salad.

eat.title: Gulasch
eat.creator: Beef stewed with onions and paprika
eat.why: A Hungarian herdsman’s dish that became the standby of every Viennese inn and army kitchen.

eat.title: Kaiserschmarrn
eat.creator: A thick torn pancake with raisins, dusted with sugar, with plum compote
eat.why: The emperor’s mess. One story says it was made for Franz Joseph when a dessert went wrong.

drink.title: A melange
drink.creator: With a glass of water on a small silver tray
drink.why: The spoon is balanced across the water glass. The water is refilled without your asking.

drink.title: A white wine spritzer
drink.creator: Young wine with soda water
drink.why: The drink of the Heuriger gardens on a summer evening.

drink.title: Tokaji
drink.creator: Sweet golden wine from north-east Hungary
drink.why: Called the wine of kings and the king of wines. The court sent it as a diplomatic present.

drink.title: Apfelschorle
drink.creator: Apple juice with sparkling water
drink.why: The everyday summer drink of Austria and Germany: apple juice mixed half and half with fizzy mineral water. Drink it cold, in a tall glass.

customs.title: Titles
customs.creator: Herr Doktor, Frau Hofrat
customs.why: People are addressed by their degree or rank, and a wife by her husband’s. It is still done in Austria, half seriously.

customs.title: Staying
customs.creator: The coffeehouse table is yours
customs.why: No waiter will bring a bill until asked. To be hurried would be an insult.

customs.title: The ball season
customs.creator: From New Year to Shrove Tuesday
customs.why: Young couples in white open each ball with a polonaise, and at midnight everyone dances a quadrille.

customs.title: Washing of the feet
customs.creator: On Maundy Thursday
customs.why: Each year the emperor knelt and washed the feet of twelve poor old men of Vienna, then served them a meal with his own hands.

games.title: Tarock
games.creator: Card game · Austria and Hungary
games.why: A family of trick-taking games played with fifty-four cards, twenty-two of them trumps. Every coffeehouse had its tables, and every regiment its school.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game
games.why: Vienna’s cafes were among the chess capitals of the world. Trotsky played daily at the Café Central before 1914.

games.title: Schnapsen
games.creator: Card game · Austria
games.why: A fast game for two with twenty cards, the object being to reach sixty-six points first. The game of every country inn.

games.title: Carambole billiards
games.creator: Table game
games.why: Three balls and no pockets. The better coffeehouses kept several tables in a back room.

festivals.title: The New Year’s Concert
festivals.creator: 1 January, in the Musikverein, Vienna
festivals.why: The Vienna Philharmonic plays waltzes and polkas by the Strauss family, broadcast to some ninety countries.

festivals.title: The Vienna Opera Ball
festivals.creator: The Thursday before Ash Wednesday
festivals.why: The State Opera’s stalls are floored over, and five thousand guests dance until five in the morning.

festivals.title: The Emperor’s Birthday
festivals.creator: 18 August, at Bad Ischl
festivals.why: The spa town where Franz Joseph spent eighty-three summers still marks the day with a mass and a parade of bands in old uniforms.

places.title: The Hofburg
places.creator: Vienna, Austria
places.why: The imperial apartments, with Franz Joseph’s iron bed and standing desk, and the Treasury with the crowns of two empires.

places.title: Schönbrunn
places.creator: Vienna, Austria
places.why: The yellow summer palace of Maria Theresa, with its garden, its hilltop pavilion and the oldest zoo in the world. The colour gave its name to a shade used on public buildings across the monarchy.

places.title: The Imperial Crypt
places.creator: Capuchin Church, Vienna, Austria
places.why: A hundred and fifty Habsburgs lie here in metal coffins, from the extravagant double tomb of Maria Theresa to the plain one of Joseph II.

places.title: Café Sperl
places.creator: Gumpendorfer Strasse 11, Vienna, Austria
places.why: Opened in 1880 and hardly altered: bentwood chairs, marble tables, billiards, newspapers and waiters in black.

places.title: Bad Ischl
places.creator: Salzkammergut, Austria
places.why: The small spa among mountains where the emperor became engaged, hunted every summer and signed the declaration of war in 1914. His villa is open.

places.title: Trieste
places.creator: Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Italy
places.why: The monarchy’s seaport: Italian in speech, Viennese in its coffeehouses and offices, with the white castle of Miramare on the shore.

ethics.title: Duty
ethics.text: Do the work that falls to you, daily, whether or not anyone thanks you.
ethics.practice: Finish today the thing you are responsible for and least want to do.

ethics.title: Courtesy
ethics.text: Politeness makes it possible for very different people to share a city.
ethics.practice: Use a formal greeting and a title with someone you usually treat casually.

ethics.title: Tolerance
ethics.text: Joseph II granted freedom of worship in 1781. Living together begins with leaving people alone.
ethics.practice: Let someone do a thing their way without comment.

ethics.title: Moderation
ethics.text: The empire’s wisdom was to settle for the bearable compromise.
ethics.practice: In a dispute today, propose the solution with which no one is delighted and all can live.

ethics.title: Cultivation
ethics.text: A person should read the papers, hear music, know some history and speak more than one language.
ethics.practice: Learn one thing today for no practical reason.

ethics.title: Constancy
ethics.text: The same desk, the same cafe, the same walk. There is strength in a regular life.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today at exactly the hour you did it yesterday.

philosophy.title: An empire of many peoples
philosophy.text: The monarchy was not a nation and did not try to be. Loyalty was to a dynasty and a shared order, across eleven languages.
philosophy.practice: What holds a community together when it has no single culture?

philosophy.title: If it did not exist
philosophy.text: A Czech patriot argued that the small peoples between Germany and Russia needed a common roof, and that without Austria they would be swallowed one by one. He was proved right after 1918.
philosophy.practice: What imperfect arrangement in your life protects more than you notice?

philosophy.title: Marriage over war
philosophy.text: The Habsburgs gained most of their lands at the altar. Patience and alliance can win what force cannot.
philosophy.practice: What could you gain by joining forces that you are trying to win by a fight?

philosophy.title: Muddling through
philosophy.text: The monarchy survived for centuries by never fully solving anything. It adjusted, postponed and compromised.
philosophy.practice: Is there a problem you should stop trying to solve and simply manage?

philosophy.title: Form
philosophy.text: Titles, uniforms and ceremony gave people a place and a way to behave. Form can be empty, and it can also be a shelter.
philosophy.practice: Which of your routines is holding you up?

philosophy.title: The golden age of security
philosophy.text: Zweig’s parents believed that progress was assured and the future insured. Within a generation everything was gone.
philosophy.practice: What do you assume is permanent?

philosophy.title: Alone in company
philosophy.text: The coffeehouse offered a third thing between solitude and society: one’s own table in a full room.
philosophy.practice: Where can you be alone among people?

philosophy.title: Gay apocalypse
philosophy.text: Vienna around 1900 produced Freud, Mahler, Klimt, Schoenberg and Wittgenstein while its politics decayed. A critic called the city a laboratory for the end of the world.
philosophy.practice: What is flowering around you, and what is rotting?

intro: The Habsburgs took their name from a castle on a hill in what is now northern Switzerland. In 1273 the German princes, wanting a king too weak to trouble them, elected Count Rudolf of Habsburg. He surprised them by defeating the king of Bohemia and taking the duchies of Austria for his family. They kept them for 640 years.

They were not great conquerors. Their gift was for marriage, patience and survival. Around 1500 three weddings in a row brought them the Netherlands, then Spain with its new American empire, then Bohemia and Hungary. A Latin verse summed it up: let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry. Charles V, who inherited most of this, ruled lands on which, it was said, the sun never set. He divided them, and from 1556 there were two branches. The Spanish line died out in 1700. The Austrian line held central Europe.

For two centuries their main task was to defend it, against the Ottomans, who twice besieged Vienna, and against Protestant revolt and French ambition. After the Turkish siege of 1683 was broken, the monarchy expanded down the Danube and Vienna was rebuilt in the baroque. In the eighteenth century Maria Theresa, who had to fight for her inheritance as a woman, and her son Joseph II reformed it from above: compulsory schooling for all children, an honest professional civil service, the end of serfdom, and freedom of worship for Protestants, Orthodox and Jews.

What emerged was something unique in Europe. It was not a nation. It was a collection of kingdoms and provinces, with a dozen peoples and faiths, held together by a dynasty, an army, a bureaucracy and the Catholic Church, and later by railways, schools and a shared way of life. From Lviv to Trieste one found the same yellow-painted stations and offices, the same coffeehouses with the same newspapers, the same pastries, uniforms and forms of address.

In the nineteenth century nationalism made this harder each decade. The young Franz Joseph came to the throne in the revolution of 1848 and reigned until 1916. Defeated by Prussia, he came to terms with the Hungarians in 1867 and created the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary. He rose before dawn, slept on an iron bed, and read his files. His brother was shot in Mexico, his only son killed himself, his wife was murdered. Around him Vienna, Budapest and Prague became some of the most brilliant cities in the world, the homes of Mahler, Klimt, Freud, Kafka and Bartók.

On 28 June 1914 his heir was assassinated at Sarajevo. The war the monarchy began in response destroyed it. In the autumn of 1918 its peoples declared their independence one after another, and the last emperor, Karl, withdrew. Seven states arose on its territory.

Many who lived through what followed came to look back on the old monarchy as a lost world of security and tolerance. That is partly nostalgia. This Onda takes from it the habits that made its daily life: duty done early, a courteous word, another language, an unhurried coffee, a walk and music at home.
guide.origin: A castle in what is now Switzerland, then Vienna, and lands from the North Sea to the Carpathians
guide.era: Rudolf of Habsburg was elected king in 1273. The last emperor withdrew from government on 11 November 1918

figures.name: Rudolf I
figures.bio: The count who became king and won Austria. He is said to have given his horse to a priest carrying the sacrament, a story the family told for centuries.

figures.name: Maximilian I
figures.bio: The last knight and the first modern publicist, who arranged the marriages that made his grandsons masters of half of Europe.

figures.name: Charles V
figures.bio: Ruler of Spain, the Netherlands, much of Italy, the German empire and the Americas. Worn out, he abdicated and retired to a monastery.

figures.name: Rudolf II
figures.bio: A melancholy collector who moved the court to Prague and filled it with astronomers, alchemists and painters, Kepler and Arcimboldo among them.

figures.name: Maria Theresa
figures.bio: The only woman to rule the Habsburg lands. She bore sixteen children, fought two long wars and founded the monarchy’s schools and administration.

figures.name: Joseph II
figures.bio: Her son, the impatient reformer, who issued some six thousand decrees in ten years and asked for the epitaph: here lies a prince whose intentions were pure, and who saw all his plans fail.

figures.name: Prince Metternich
figures.bio: The chancellor who presided over the Congress of Vienna and for thirty years kept Europe at peace and its liberals under watch.

figures.name: Franz Schubert
figures.bio: A schoolmaster’s son who wrote some six hundred songs and died at thirty-one. He hardly left Vienna and was hardly known outside his circle of friends.

figures.name: Franz Joseph I
figures.bio: Emperor for sixty-eight years. Dutiful, unimaginative and personally modest, he became the one thing all his peoples had in common.

figures.name: Elisabeth
figures.bio: His Bavarian wife, known as Sisi. Beautiful, restless and unhappy at court, she championed Hungary, wrote poetry and was stabbed by an anarchist in Geneva.

figures.name: Johann Strauss II
figures.bio: The waltz king, who conducted with his violin in his hand and made Viennese dance music known from Boston to St Petersburg.

figures.name: Karl I
figures.bio: The last emperor, who tried in secret to make peace in 1917. He died in exile on Madeira.

history.detail: Rudolf is elected King of the Romans, defeats Ottokar of Bohemia in 1278 and grants Austria and Styria to his sons.
Burgundy and the Netherlands come with Mary of Burgundy, Spain with Joanna of Castile, and Bohemia and Hungary when the young king Louis falls fighting the Turks at Mohács.
Ottoman armies twice reach the walls. The second siege is broken on 12 September 1683 by a relief army under the king of Poland.
An Armenian merchant, Johannes Diodato, is given the first licence to serve coffee in Vienna.
She defends her succession, loses Silesia to Prussia, and orders in 1774 that every child from six to twelve shall go to school.
Joseph II grants freedom of worship to Lutherans, Calvinists and Orthodox, eases restrictions on Jews and abolishes personal serfdom.
Franz II proclaims himself Emperor of Austria and, under pressure from Napoleon, lays down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire.
The powers redraw the map of Europe between balls and dinners. The settlement keeps the general peace for a century.
Risings in Vienna, Prague, Budapest and Milan nearly end the monarchy. Metternich flees, and the eighteen-year-old Franz Joseph becomes emperor.
The emperor orders the city walls demolished. A boulevard of public buildings and private palaces rises in their place.
After defeat by Prussia, Hungary receives its own government and parliament. Franz Joseph is crowned its king in Budapest.
Crown Prince Rudolf shoots his young mistress and himself at a hunting lodge. Nine years later the empress is murdered.
The heir, Franz Ferdinand, and his wife are shot by a Bosnian Serb student. A month later the monarchy declares war on Serbia.
With the army dissolving, Karl signs a statement renouncing any part in affairs of state. Austria is declared a republic the next day.

concepts.detail: The lands had nothing in common but their ruler. Each was held by a separate title, and the emperor’s full style ran to several dozen.

Frederick III marked his possessions with the five vowels in the fifteenth century. The usual readings are that Austria is destined to rule the whole world, or that Austria will last to the end of time.
The law of 1713 that declared the lands inseparable and allowed a daughter to inherit them. Maria Theresa had to defend it in arms.

concepts.text: Everything for the people, nothing by them.
concepts.detail: Reform ordered from the throne by rulers who believed the state existed for the welfare of its subjects and did not consult them.
After 1867 Austria and Hungary shared only the ruler, the army, foreign policy and the finances for those, renegotiated every ten years.
No group was a majority. Language rights in schools, courts and offices became the main business of politics, argued out bench by bench.
Open to anyone for the price of a cup. Its newspapers, heating and writing materials made it the workplace of people with small rooms and large ideas.
Between 1815 and 1848, barred from politics, the middle classes turned to the home, to music, walking and friendship. A style and a state of mind.
Within a few streets and years: psychoanalysis, twelve-tone music, the Secession, modern architecture, logical philosophy and political Zionism.

facts.text: Franz Joseph reigned for sixty-seven years and 355 days, longer than any European monarch then living could remember.
The imperial anthem was sung in at least eleven official languages, to Haydn’s tune.
The croissant’s ancestor, the crescent-shaped kipferl, is Viennese. Legend ties it to the siege of 1683.
The monarchy’s banknotes carried their value in ten languages.
When a Habsburg was buried, the herald knocked at the crypt door and was refused admission until he announced the dead only as a poor sinner.
The dye called Schönbrunn yellow coloured stations and barracks from the Alps to what is now Ukraine.

sensitivity.note: The Habsburg Monarchy is remembered fondly in some of its former lands and resentfully in others. This Onda borrows the civil habits of its towns. It is partly a portrait of a world seen through nostalgia, and says so.
requiredCaveats: Czechs, Hungarians, Poles, Ukrainians, Italians, South Slavs and Romanians each remember Habsburg rule differently, and many fought to leave it.
The golden age of security was golden for the middle and upper classes. Vienna around 1900 also had some of the worst housing in Europe.
The city that gave Jews civil equality also elected an openly antisemitic mayor in 1897, and the young Hitler learned his politics there.
